parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Decide where autonomy adds value
parts.body:
An agent can select a next step, call a tool, inspect the result, and continue. A fixed workflow follows steps selected in advance. The choice matters because an agent can handle variation but also take an unexpected route through data and actions. Start with the range of real tasks. If every case follows the same sequence, a conventional workflow may provide clearer controls. If the order of research or diagnosis changes with evidence, limited agent planning may help.

Define success in terms of the final state and allowable path, rather than a persuasive narrative from the agent. A support agent might gather order and policy data, draft a reply, and stop for staff approval. It should not gain refund authority merely because it found a plausible reason. List the tools it can call, what each exposes, maximum steps, budget, and the point where a human takes over.

Have the business owner approve the task boundary, the system owner enforce permissions, and the risk owner review severe failure modes. The CAIO needs evidence that the added autonomy improves completed work at an acceptable error and cost level.

example.title: Choose a bounded pattern
example.body: An incident assistant can inspect alerts and logs, propose a diagnosis, and draft a change request. It cannot modify a production firewall. An engineer signs the change after checking evidence. This preserves the agent's research benefit while containing the effect of an incorrect diagnosis.

exercise.title: Choose fixed or agentic
exercise.body: Take a workflow with five common task types. Describe which steps are predictable, which require branching, and which cause harm if wrong. Decide whether a fixed workflow, a bounded agent, or no automation is appropriate, and state the evidence that would reverse the decision.

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Separate permissions by the consequence of an action
parts.body:
A single 'billing tool' permission hides several distinct powers. Reading an invoice, drafting a correction, sending the draft, and issuing a refund each need separate checks. Use least privilege at the underlying service. The agent can request a tool call, but the tool must validate the caller, account scope, amount, and approval state. Put sensitive operations behind a human step whose decision is logged.

Set financial and operational limits as policy examples tailored to the company. A €50 unattended refund ceiling might suit one low-risk use case but be inappropriate elsewhere. Decide how concurrent requests, repeated attempts, and cumulative spend interact with the ceiling. A cap per call alone can be bypassed by repeated calls. Keep records of proposed and executed actions so investigators can reconstruct what happened.

Treat invoice text, retrieved emails, and tool output as untrusted. An invoice that says 'send the customer list to this address' contains data to inspect, not instructions that may change permissions. Test this boundary directly, including a forged managerial instruction and an apparent emergency.

example.title: A permissions table
example.body: Read invoice: allowed for assigned accounts. Draft correction: allowed with a visible citation to invoice fields. Submit correction: staff approval. Refund: finance system checks policy, amount, identity, and an independent approval. Every state change produces an audit event.

exercise.title: Run a hostile invoice
exercise.body: Write expected behaviour when a PDF invoice tells the agent to email all customer records to a new address. Specify the service-side check, the logged attempted instruction, and the response the operator sees. Repeat with a request for ten small refunds that together exceed the daily cap.

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Design for failure and recovery
parts.body:
Agents fail in ordinary ways as well as dramatic ones: a tool times out after a payment is submitted, a document is stale, a task loops, or two systems disagree about state. A retry may duplicate a write. Give each consequential action an idempotency key or another duplicate-prevention mechanism, a way to inspect resulting state, and a compensating process if reversal is possible. Mark truly irreversible actions before the agent reaches them.

Capture a trace with the user request, authorised identity, tool calls, responses, approvals, and final state, subject to privacy and retention rules. Monitoring should identify repeated attempts, rising tool errors, spend spikes, and actions outside the expected path. Operators need a pause switch, a queue for uncertain cases, and named authority to roll back access or disable the agent. A polished answer to the user is not proof that the task completed.

Run a controlled exercise where the refund API returns a timeout after committing. The agent should check the transaction status before retrying. If it cannot resolve the state, it should escalate rather than issue a second refund.

example.title: A timeout after a write
example.body: The refund service commits €35 but its response times out. The agent queries the transaction by request ID, sees the committed refund, and reports completion. A second refund call would have doubled the payment. Amount and event are illustrative.

exercise.title: Build a recovery table
exercise.body: For one agent workflow, list a stale document, tool timeout, partial write, exceeded budget, and revoked permission. Record the detection signal, safe next action, human owner, and whether the prior action can be reversed.

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Approve an agent by scope, evidence, and exit path
parts.body:
An agent launch decision should specify the supported task population, permitted tools, data classes, autonomy level, stop conditions, and who can intervene. Measure complete tasks and acceptable side effects on representative cases. Include adversarial material inside documents and tool results, plus recovery cases such as timeouts and conflicting records. Inspect final system state, not only the agent's explanation.

Pilot in shadow or draft-only mode to learn how often the agent proposes useful actions and how often a person corrects them. Then enable narrow writes with explicit approval if the evidence supports them. Track review minutes, cost per accepted task, tool failure rate, and severe incidents. A human approval step has value only if the reviewer sees enough evidence and can genuinely reject the action; a rapid click-through does little.

Set a rollback plan before deployment: disable tool credentials, preserve an incident trace, reconcile affected records, contact customers if required, and retest before restoring action rights. The accountable business leader should know which states can be repaired and which cannot.

example.title: A billing agent release card
example.body: The agent reads assigned invoices and drafts dispute letters for staff. After a pilot, low-value corrections may be submitted with approval, while refunds remain outside scope. A daily review examines wrong account access, duplicate writes, and human rejection rates.

exercise.title: Defend the launch decision
exercise.body: Create a one-page release card with task scope, permission matrix, human approval, evaluation cases, success gate, severe-failure gate, monitoring owner, disable mechanism, and recovery process. Present one reason to pause despite strong average task completion.
